title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
titleZh: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
author: jcubic
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.See hacker news for discussion

comments.author: jrmg
comments.textRawHtml:
In the United States the Copyright Office actually has guidance on this that I feel most people aren’t aware of.

https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intell...

An excerpt, with emphasis mine:

• Questions of copyrightability and AI can be resolved pursuant to existing law, without the need for legislative change.

• The use of AI tools to assist rather than stand in for human creativity does not affect the availability of copyright protection for the output.

• Copyright protects the original expression in a work created by a human author, even if the work also includes AI-generated material.

• Copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements.

• Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.

• Based on the functioning of current generally available technology, prompts do not alone provide sufficient control.

• Human authors are entitled to copyright in their works of authorship that are perceptible in AI-generated outputs, as well as the creative selection, coordination, or arrangement of material in the outputs, or creative modifications of the outputs.

• The case has not been made for additional copyright or sui generis protection for AI- generated content.

I am sure there will be many more legal battles and probably legislation about this to come.

children.author: bilbo0s
children.textRawHtml:
Everyone should have an engineering notebook. A lot of people will find out the hard way that engineering notebooks are just table stakes in the new era.

Having said that, it's important to point out, at least as far as attorneys have advised me, that notebooks do not protect you from copyright claims if an LLM generates a section of your code that is a verbatim (or near verbatim) copy of already copyrighted code. So if you're using llm's to generate something similar to some open source project somewhere, tread lightly. I assume using llm's to generate something similar to some proprietary software package would be less of an issue since the llm would never have had access to that software's codebase in any case.

children.author: Buttons840
children.textRawHtml:
Who broke the copyright though? Me who unknowingly copied some code from a webpage that gave me permission to do so, or the webpage that stole it from somebody else?

I guess both?

In this case, the "webpage" is some frontier AI compnay and a trillion dollars of investor money or whatever, so I guess they won't be held responsible, but I might, even though I'm arguably guilty of a far lesser crime.

children.author: tredre3
children.textRawHtml:
I suppose part of the issue is that you're knowingly and willingly use/buy code that you know to be stolen. There doesn't seem to be any ambiguity in your mind, you used the word "stole" yourself.

Thus in some sense it's like purchasing stolen goods in real life. Sure it's a lesser crime than stealing it yourself. But doing so knowingly is still a crime almost everywhere.
